translations.text: And now I will tell you truly about the end of the holy and blessed Shushanik.

It was in the eighth year of the [?] of the king of the Persians that Varsken the pitiakhsh, son of Arshusha, set out for the royal court. For he too had formerly been a Christian, born of a Christian father and mother.
And his wife was the daughter of Vardan, commander of the Armenians, concerning whom I have written this to you. Her name, after her father, was Vardan,
and out of affection she was called Shushanik. As we have said, she had feared God from her youth.
And she always grieved in her heart over her husband's wicked character, and she begged everyone to pray for him,
so that God might change him from that senseless character and he might come to the understanding of Christ.
But as for this wretched and thrice-pitiable Varsken, utterly lost, who could describe how he cast away the blessed hope of Christ?!
Or who would not weep for him, who had seen neither affliction, nor fear, nor the sword, nor imprisonment for Christ's sake?!
For when he stood before the king of the Persians, it was not to receive honor;
rather, he offered himself as a gift to that king by denying the true God, and he worshipped fire, for he cast himself away from Christ in every respect.
And this pitiable man asked the king of the Persians for a wife, so that he might please the king, and he spoke to him thus:
"My lawful wife and my children, I will convert them too to your religion, just as I have been converted."
He promised this, though he had no such assurance from Shushanik. Then the king rejoiced and commanded that the king's daughter be given to him as wife.
And the pitiakhsh departed from the king of the Persians. And when he reached the borders of Kartli, in the land of Hereti, he made a plan
to send word so that the nobles, his sons and his servants would come out to meet him, so that he might enter the country with them as a loyal subject.
And he sent his servant ahead on a post horse to go to the village called Tsurtavi.
And when he arrived, he went in before Shushanik, our queen, and greeted her.
But the blessed Shushanik said to him, as if prophesying: "If he is alive in spirit, may you both live, he and you.
If you are dead in spirit, let that greeting of yours return to you."
But the man did not dare to speak to her. Then holy Shushanik made him swear an oath and questioned him closely.
And the man told the truth and said: "Varsken has denied the true God."
When the blessed Shushanik heard this, she fell to the ground and beat her head [?], and with bitter tears she said:
"Wretched Varsken has become pitiable, for he has denied the true God, professed the fire (atroshan), and joined himself to the godless."
And she rose and left her palace and in the fear of God went into the church. And she took with her his three sons and one daughter and presented them before the altar.
And thus she prayed and said: "Lord God, they were given by you, and may you protect them,
enlightened by the holy font through the grace of the Holy Spirit, to be one flock of one shepherd, our Lord Jesus Christ."
And when they had finished the hour of vespers, she found a small little house near the church and went into it, full of bitterness. She leaned against a corner and wept with bitter tears.
But the bishop of the pitiakhsh's household, whose name was Apots, was not there. He had gone to the monastery of a certain holy man to ask about some matter.
And I too, the priest of Queen Shushanik, was with that bishop.
And at once a deacon came to us from home and told us all of this: the arrival of the pitiakhsh and what the queen had done.
And we were filled with grief and wept with great weeping, embittered because our sins had been brought to light.
And I mounted early and reached the village where the blessed Shushanik was.
And when I saw her embittered, I too wept with her, and I said to the blessed Shushanik:
"You are about to enter a great contest, queen. Guard the faith of Christ, so that the enemy does not find pasture in you like a moth.
And holy Shushanik said to me: "Priest, I too am prepared for a great contest." And I said to her:
"So it is: be brave, patient and long-suffering." But she said to me: "These afflictions are for me alone!"
And I said to her: "Your affliction is our affliction, and your joy is our joy. You were not only our queen, but you looked upon all of us as your children."
And I said to the blessed one in secret: "Tell me what you intend, so that I may know it and write down your labour."
But she said to me: "Why do you ask me this?" And I answered and said to her: "Do you stand firm?" And she said to me:
"Far be it from me to share in the deeds and sins of Varsken." I answered and said to her:
"He has a bitter mind; he will subject you to beatings and great torment." But she said to me:
"It is better for me to die at his hands than for him and me to be united and my soul to be lost;
for I have heard from Paul the apostle: a brother or a sister is not bound, but let them separate." And I said: "So it is."
And while we were in this conversation, a certain Persian man came. He went in before the blessed Shushanik and said with weeping:
"How has such a house of peace become so pitiable, and joy been turned into grief?"
But he was acting on Varsken's advice and said this with deceit, and he wanted to entrap the blessed one.
The saint recognized his deceitful intent and guarded herself firmly.
And after three days Varsken the pitiakhsh came. And that Persian spoke to him in secret and said:
"As I have found out, your wife has turned away from you. I tell you, do not say any harsh word to her, for the nature of women is narrow."
And the next day, when the pitiakhsh got up, he called for us priests, and we went.
And he greeted us with joy and said to us: "Now do not be shy of me at all, and do not loathe me any longer." And we answered and said:
"You have destroyed yourself, and you have destroyed us too." Only then did he begin to speak, and he said: "How did my wife dare to do such a thing against me?
Now go and tell her: 'You have overthrown my image, you have poured ashes on my bed, you have left your place and gone elsewhere.'"
But holy Shushanik said: "It was not I who set up that image, that I should be the one to overthrow it.
Rather, your father set up martyrs' shrines and built churches, and you have undone your father's works and turned his good deeds into something else.
Your father brought saints into his house, but you have brought in demons.
He confessed and believed in the God of heaven and earth, but you have denied the true God and worship fire. And as you have denied your Creator, so I too have despised you.
And even if you bring many tortures upon me, I will have no part in your deeds."
We reported all this to the pitiakhsh. He grew angry at heart and raged against her.
Then he sent Jojik, his brother, and Jojik's wife, his sister-in-law, and the bishop of his household, and said to them:
"Tell her this: 'Get up and come to your own place, and do not hold to such a mind! If you do not, I will drag you here by force.'"
When they arrived, they went in before the queen and spoke many persuasive words to her. Then holy Shushanik said to them:
"Wise men, you speak well, but do not believe that I would ever be his wife again.
I thought that I would turn him to my side and he would confess the true God, and now you are forcing me to do this? Far be this from me!
And you, Jojik, are no longer my brother-in-law, nor am I any longer your brother's wife, nor is your wife my sister, since you are on his side and share in his deeds."
Jojik said to her: "I know that they have now sent servants, and he will have you dragged away." But holy Shushanik said:
"If he binds me and drags me, I rejoice, for in that way the judgment [?] concerning me will come from him."
And when they heard this from her, they all wept, and Jojik got up and went outside in tears.
Then holy Shushanik said to the bishop: "How can you tell me to give in, when he has denied God?"
But Jojik pleaded with her and said: "You are our sister; do not ruin this queenly house." Holy Shushanik said to him:
"I know that I am your sister and that we were brought up together, but I cannot do that, even if bloodshed should come of it, and all of you will be answerable for it."
And as they pressed her very hard, holy and blessed Shushanik got up, took her Gospel with her, and weeping said this:
"Lord God, you know that I go to death with all my heart."
Having said this, she went with them, and she took with her her Gospel and the holy books of the martyrs.
When she entered the palace, she did not sit in her own upper chamber, but in a small cell.
And holy Shushanik raised her hands to heaven and said:
"Lord God, not one merciful person was found among the priests, nor did any layman come forward among this people, but all of them have handed me over to death to Varsken, the enemy of God."
Two days later the wolf came to the palace and said to his servants:
"Today Jojik, his wife and I will eat bread together, but let no one else be allowed to come in with us."
And when evening came, they called Jojik's wife and wanted to eat together, so that they might bring holy Shushanik as well.
And when the hour of the meal came, Jojik and his wife went in before holy Shushanik so that they might get her to eat bread too,
For she had spent all those days fasting. When they pressed her very hard, they brought her to the palace with difficulty.
But she tasted nothing. Then Jojik's wife offered her wine in a cup and kept urging her to drink at least that.
Holy Shushanik said to her in anger: "When has it ever happened until now that men and women ate bread together?!"
And she thrust out her hand, smashed the cup against her face, and the wine spilled.
Then Varsken began to abuse her shamefully and trampled her with his feet. He took a poker and struck her on the head, gashing it deeply, and made one of her eyes swell up.
He struck her face mercilessly with his fist and dragged her about by the hair. He shrieked like a raging beast and roared like a madman.
Then his brother Jojik rose to intervene, and they struggled until Jojik too was beaten, and Varsken even struck him on the head with a kubasti [?]. With difficulty, like a lamb from a wolf,
he took her out of his hands. Holy Shushanik lay on the ground as though dead, and Varsken cursed her family and lineage and called her a destroyer of the house.
And he ordered that she be bound and that fetters be put on her feet.
When his anger had calmed a little, that Persian came and fervently begged him to release holy Shushanik from her bonds.
And because he begged so much, Varsken ordered that she be released, brought into a cell, and carefully guarded by a single servant,
And he ordered that no one else should go in to see her, neither man nor woman.
As soon as it was dawn, he asked his servant: "How is she after those wounds?"
The servant said to him: "She cannot recover." Then he went in himself and saw her, and he was astonished at how badly she was swollen.
He gave the servant an order, saying: "Let no one go in to see her." And he himself went off to hunt.
Then I got up and went and said to the guard: "Let me in alone, so that I may see her wound." But he said to me:
"What if he finds out and kills me?" And I said to him: "Wretch, were you not brought up by her? And even if he kills you for her sake, what of it?!"
Then he let me in secretly. When I went inside, I saw her face cracked open and swollen, and I cried aloud and wept.
But holy Shushanik said to me: "Do not weep for me, for this night has been the beginning of joy for me." And I said to holy Shushanik:
"Let me wash the blood from your face and the ashes that have been scattered into your eyes, and put salve and medicine on you, so that perhaps you may be healed!"
But holy Shushanik said to me: "Priest, do not say that, for this blood cleanses my sins."
Then I urged her a little to take the food that Bishop Samuel and John had sent, for they were secretly looking after her and comforting her. Then holy Shushanik said to me:
"Priest, I cannot taste anything, for my jaws and some of my teeth are broken."
Then I took a little wine and bread and soaked it, and she tasted a little.
I was hurrying to leave. Then holy Shushanik said to me: "Priest, shall I send him back these ornaments of his?
He may be asking for them, for I no longer have any use for them in this life." But I said: "Don't hurry over anything; let them stay with you."
And while we were still discussing this, a youth came and said: "Is Jacob there?!" And I said:
"What do you want?" And he said to me: "The pitiakhsh is summoning you." And I wondered why he should be summoning me at this hour.
And I hurried and went. And he said to me: "You know, priest, that I am going off to fight against the Huns.
And I will not leave my jewellery to her, since she is not my wife. Someone [else] will be found who will wear it out.
Go and bring all of it back to me, whatever there is." So I went and told holy Shushanik.
And she rejoiced greatly and gave thanks to God, and she sent everything to me, and I took it to the pitiakhsh.
And he received it from me, looked it over, and found everything accounted for. And again he said: "Later someone will be found who will adorn herself with this."
When the Great Fast arrived, the blessed Shushanik went to a place near the holy church, looked for a small cell, and shut herself up there.
And there was a small window in that cell, and she blocked it up. And she remained in that darkness, fasting, praying and weeping.
And one of the pitiakhsh's own men said to him: "Say nothing to her during these holy fasts."
When the Monday of the Completion arrived and the pitiakhsh came back from the war against the Huns, the devil was digging at his heart.
And he got up and went to the church and said to Bishop Aputsa: "Give me back my wife; why are you separating her from me?"
And he began to curse and to blaspheme God savagely. But one priest said to him:
"Lord, why do you act like this and say such evil things, and curse the bishop, and speak to holy Shushanik in anger?
But he struck that priest on the back with a staff, and the priest no longer dared to speak.
And so he dragged holy Shushanik through the mud and over thorns from the church all the way to the palace, dragging her as if she were a corpse.
And in places brambles were spread on the ground, and her own feet were set down on those brambles, and Shushanik's garments and flesh were torn to small shreds by the brambles.
And so they brought her to the palace, and he ordered her to be bound and beaten. He reviled her and said:
"See, your church has not helped you, nor have those backers of yours, the Christians, nor their Lord."
And when they had struck her about three hundred times with a rod, no cry of pain came from her mouth, nor any groan.
Then holy Shushanik said to the lawless Varsken: "Wretch, you did not have pity on yourself, and you have turned away from God. Would you have pity on me?"
And when he saw the great amount of blood flowing down her tender flesh, he ordered a chain to be put around her neck.
And he ordered a jailer to take holy Shushanik to the fortress and shut her in a dark prison so that she would die.
A certain deacon of that bishop was standing beside holy Shushanik at the time when she was being led out of the palace, and he wanted to say to her: "Stand firm!"
But the pitiakhsh fixed his eye on him, and the deacon had no chance to say anything more. He said only "Stand f—" and fell silent, and he began to flee in haste.
Then they led her out, and holy Shushanik was taken away barefoot and with her hair hanging loose, like one of the disgraced,
and no one dared to cover her head, because the pitiakhsh followed close behind her on horseback and reviled her with many insults.
And a great crowd of women and men went along with the saint, a countless multitude, for they followed behind her,
they raised their voices and wept, and tore their cheeks, and pitifully shed their tears for holy Shushanik.
But the holy Shushanik looked back at the people and said to them: "Do not weep, my brothers and my sisters and my children, but remember me in your prayers.
And from now on I am parted from you, for you will not see me come out of the fortress alive again."
And when the pitiakhsh saw the uproar and the weeping of the men and women, the old and the young, he rode back and forth on horseback, driving them off, and put them all to flight.
And when they reached the bridge of the fortress, the pitiakhsh said to holy Shushanik:
"This is the only time you will walk in on your own feet, for you will not come out alive again unless four men carry you out."
And when they entered the fortress, they found a small room on the north side, small and dark, and there they put the saint.
And the chain that was on her neck stayed there, and the lawless Varsken sealed it with his own seal.
But the holy Shushanik said: "I am glad of this, that I may be tormented here and find rest there." And the pitiakhsh said to her: "Yes, yes, rest!"
Then he set guards over her and ordered them to kill her by starvation. And he spoke to them like this:
"I tell you: if anyone goes in to her, man or woman, look out for yourselves, and for your wives and children and houses. I will be blameless for whatever I do to you."
Then he came out of the fortress. And on the third Sunday he summoned one of the guards, questioned him and said: "Is that wretched woman still alive even now?" And he said to him:
"Lord, she is to be reckoned closer to death than to life, for she is dying, above all from hunger, since she takes no food at all."
And he said to him: "Do not worry about anything. Leave her alone; let her die."
But I spoke to that guard with many entreaties and promised him a drinking vessel.
And only with difficulty did he agree to let me in, and he said to me: "When night falls, come by yourself alone."
And when the guard brought me in, I saw that lamb of Christ, beautiful like a bride, adorned with the fetters. And since my heart could not bear it, I wept greatly.
But the holy Shushanik said to me: "Are you weeping over this good thing, priest?" And the guard said to me: "If I had known this, I would not have let you in."
Then I began to speak to her and strengthen her, as much as God gave me to say. And I took leave of her and went quickly to my dwelling.
Now the pitiakhsh had set out for Chor, and Jojik, his brother, was not present when this was done to the holy Shushanik. And when Jojik arrived, he followed after the pitiakhsh.
And he caught up with him at the borders of Hereti and begged him earnestly to order her release from the fetters.
And as he was greatly grieved, he ordered that she be released only from the bonds.
And when Jojik came, he took the chain off her neck. But the holy Shushanik would not let the fetters be removed, right up to her end.
For she spent six years in that fortress and lived by a godly discipline:
with fasting, constant vigil, standing upright in prayer, tireless prostrations, and reading books without wearying.
She made that whole fortress bright and beautiful with that spiritual harp.
And from then on her deeds became known throughout all Kartli. And men and women came to offer their vows, and whatever anyone needed
was granted to them through the holy prayer of the blessed Shushanik, which God, the lover of mankind, gave her: a child to the childless, healing to the sick, sight to the eyes of the blind.
There was a certain woman, a Persian Magian, who suffered from an issue of blood, and she came to the holy Shushanik.
And Shushanik taught her to give up Magianism and become a Christian. And the woman agreed very quickly.
And she taught the woman and said to her: "Go to Jerusalem, and you will be cleansed of your issue of blood."
And he eagerly accepted it and set out on the road in the name of our God Jesus Christ, and he was healed of his illness.
And when he turned back with great joy and arrived there again, he came to give thanks for the grace of holy Shushanik, and went to his home rejoicing and healed.
But holy Shushanik, instead of needlework, took the Psalter into her hands with great eagerness, and after a few days she had learned the hundred and fifty psalms,
with which, day and night, she offered with tears that pleasing hymn to the King on high.
And they told blessed Shushanik: "He has turned your children to Magianism."
Then she began to bow down before God with great weeping, and she struck her head on the ground, sighed, and said:
"I thank you, O Lord my God, for they were never mine; they were given by you.
As you wish, let your will be done, O Lord, and keep me safe from the works of the enemy."
And I went and saw the holy Shushanik, wasted away and swollen from weeping.
And the holy bishop had sent her food, and when I urged her strongly, she tasted only a little, and we gave thanks to God.
And until that time her children used to come to see their mother. But once they had been turned and had denied God, they no longer dared to see her. Indeed, she even loathed hearing their name.
And then the pitiakhsh sent messengers and said to her: "Either do my will and come to the palace,
or, if you do not come inside, I will send you to Chor or to the court under guard." But holy Shushanik answered him thus:
"Wretched and senseless man, if you send me to the court or to Chor, who knows whether I may meet with some good there and escape this evil."
And the pitiakhsh said in his heart, about the words the guard had told him: "Who knows whether I may come upon some good fortune," namely:
"Perhaps I may take a wife from among the princes' families [?]." And from then on he sent no one to her any more.
But holy Shushanik spoke of enduring those cruel beatings, so that she might please God.
Then the pitiakhsh chose her own foster-brother to bring her to the palace. And when that man said to her:
"Listen to me and come down to the palace, and do not ruin this house of yours," holy Shushanik said to him:
"Tell that godless man: You beat me and said to me, 'You shall not come out of [?] that fortress on living feet.'
But now, if you are able to raise the dead, first raise your own mother, who is buried at Urdi.
But if you cannot raise her, neither can you bring me out, unless you drag me out."
And when they reported those words to the pitiakhsh, he said: "Truly, I did say that!"
On the next day someone came in and said to holy Shushanik:
"You answered him well with that word, for he meant to deceive you that way, and in his heart he had conceived another plan, an evil one, against you," holy Shushanik said to him.
"And do not think that God is asleep, he who prepares the words in a person's mouth, for the Lord himself says: I will give answer in your stead."
And as the sixth year in that prison was coming to its end, sickness and illness came upon her because of her excessive zeal in the labours of her fortitude,
about which I had cried out to her beforehand, telling her: "Do not do too much, for you will be a heavy burden on that body of yours,
for it will not hold out for you, and then you will no longer be able to do any good work at all, with such harsh fasting, constant standing, and toil all night long in psalms and hymns."
But she gave her body no rest anywhere, not even a little, and she wasted away and melted like ash.
During the great fasts of fulfilment, those forty days, throughout the six years she never sat down, neither by day nor by night,
nor did she sleep, nor did she take any food, except that on the Lord's day only she partook of the body and blood of Christ our God,
and she took only a little broth made from greens, and even that only a little, but she did not taste bread until the end of the fast.
And from the day they imprisoned her in that fortress, she did not lay her head on a pillow, but laid down a single mud brick as her pillow.
For bedding there was one old rug, and, for people's eyes, she kept one felt cushion beside the brick pillow.
For making prostrations, one small piece of goat-hair cloth was spread beneath her, and fleas and lice beyond imagining swarmed in that place.
In summertime there was the heat of the sun, scorching like fire, and hot dry winds and harmful waters, so that even the inhabitants of that place are full of disease:
swollen with dropsy and yellowed, spotted, withered and [?], [?], with swollen faces, and living short lives;
and there is no old person in those lands. In such a fortress as this she was imprisoned for six years, and in those heavy bonds she glorified God.

And as the seventh year was beginning, wounds also came upon the body of the holy and thrice-blessed Shushanik. Because of her unceasing labours her feet swelled, and pus oozed out in place after place.
The sores were very large, and worms had settled in those sores. She took one up in her hand, showed it to me, and gave thanks to God.
And she said: "Priest, do not let this weigh on you, for the worm there is greater and does not die."
And when I saw the worms, I was more grieved than I can say and wept bitterly. Again she spoke to me in anger:
"Priest, why are you grieved? Better that these mortal worms eat me here and now in this life than that those undying worms devour me."
And I answered her: "Did the haircloth garment seem too small a torment to you, so that now you rejoice in those worms?" And she rebuked me:
"Do not tell anyone about the haircloth garment while I am alive, for soon I will leave this wretched flesh of mine."
For underneath she wore sackcloth, and no one knew of it except me, but on the outside, for people's eyes, she wore an Antiochene cloak.
When Jojik heard that the blessed queen, holy Shushanik, was near death, he set out and took with him his wife and children and his male and female servants.
And he went to the fortress to see the blessed martyr Shushanik.
And when he arrived, he forced his way in [?], bowed down before the precious cross, and greeted holy Shushanik.
He sat down beside her and asked about her pains. And the holy woman said to him:
"I am well, as God wills. But I too am going on the road that everyone must travel."
Then Jojik quickly rose up. He confessed his former lawless deeds, pleaded with holy Shushanik and said to her:
"Sister-in-law and handmaid of Christ, ask God to forgive me my many sins."
Holy Shushanik said to him: "If you did nothing otherwise than in youthful folly, God will forgive you." And Jojik said to her:
"That is why I have come to you, so that I may do nothing that does not please God." Holy Shushanik said to him:
"If you do that, you have made me immortal by those words, and may God add to the days of your life."
Then, when Jojik perceived that the saint would depart from this flesh that day, he said:
"Bless me and my wife, your handmaid, and my children and my servants and maidservants. And if we have sinned against you in anything,
"…as people of this passing world and lovers of the world, forgive us, and do not remember my stubbornness." And holy Shushanik said to Jojik and his wife:
"Be zealous [?] in this matter of mine, for no one was found among men who had mercy and pity for me, who would have persuaded that godless husband, who belongs to this passing world."
And they said to her: "Apart from you [?], we worked very hard, but he would neither listen nor speak." Then holy Shushanik said:
"Let Varsken the pitiakhsh and I be judged there, where there is no favoritism before the Judge of judges and King of kings,
where no distinction is made between man and woman, where he and I will speak with equal words before our Lord Jesus Christ.
May the Lord repay him for how he plucked my fruits before their time, quenched my lamp, withered my flower,
darkened the beauty of my goodness and brought my glory low. May God judge between him and me.
But now I thank God for this: through his torments I have found comfort, and in return for his beatings and draggings I will attain rest,
and in return for his thoughtlessness and mercilessness I await mercy from Jesus Christ my Lord."
And at all these words of hers they wept bitterly and said to her:
"Forgive us our sins and bless us, holy witness and blessed martyr of Christ God." And holy Shushanik said:
"May God forgive you for what you have done." Then she blessed Jojik, his wife, his children, his male and female servants, and all his household and palace.
She urged them to walk in the ways of God and told them: "All this life is like the flower of the fields, passing and unstable.
Whoever sowed has reaped, and whoever scattered to the poor has gathered. Whoever loses his life will find it, the one who has glorified Him."
She said farewell to them and sent them away in peace.
Then, after Jojik, Samuel, the head of the bishops, arrived with Bishop John, his companion. They had strengthened her and had been very zealous for her,
together with their households. By their presence they were [?] servants, and they were partners and sharers in her labours. With thanksgiving they sent her on toward that haven of Christ.
In the same way the great nobles and the high-born ladies, nobles and commoners of the land of Kartli, came.
Likewise those who had eagerly shared in her labours, out of her blessedness, commended her to Christ as a valiant and brave one.
And all those bishops and nobles together made one request of her:
…so that she might order the fetter from her feet [to be given] as an object of veneration [?] and a blessing for all. Concerning this, holy Shushanik said:
"What am I, this unworthy one? But because of your love of God, let the priest fulfill your wish in that matter."
As for me, what can I do? But may Christ, who is full of all things, fill you with every good thing,
you who helped me and shared in these sufferings, afflictions and torments of mine.
As for me, beloved ones, see, I am setting out on the eternal road that was prepared beforehand.
In place of this affliction of mine may Christ grant me joy, and in place of these torments, rest;
in place of these beatings, draggings and insults of mine, may I attain endless glory and honour in the heavens."
And they parted from her, full of tears, and gave glory to God for her victory. Then they came out of the fortress and left.
And the day of her calling came. She summoned Apots, the bishop of her household, and thanked him for his kindness. She entrusted me to him as to a father and foster-father,
me, this sinful and wretched man. She also entrusted to him the remains of her bones and ordered that they be laid in the place from which she had first been dragged out. And she said to him:
"If I am worthy of anything at all, I, this last worker in the vineyard who came at the eleventh hour, may you all be blessed to the end of the ages."
And she gave thanks to God and said, "Blessed is the Lord my God, for in peace I will lie down and sleep." And she gave up her spirit to the Lord, who receives all.
Then the blessed bishop John at once brought a holy shroud to wrap her holy and precious relics,
and so the rest of us lifted up the body, which was badly wasted and eaten by worms. We washed it clean of the earthy worms and the rot [?], and dressed it in that cloth [?].
And then the two bishops, John and Apots, like strong oxen who do not tire in working for that heavenly reward,
together with the whole congregation, with spiritual psalms, lit candles and fragrant incense, we took up the precious bones and carried them out to the holy church.
And we laid the holy, glorious and honoured relics of holy Shushanik to rest in the place that had been prepared.
That night we stayed awake all night like angels, and with the harp of David we glorified almighty God and his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ,
who has power over all things and toward all people. He strengthens both fathers and mothers, and to his own he grants the victory of his own might, to all who seek him with an undivided heart.
The torments of holy Shushanik began in the month of Apnisi, on the eighth of the month, on a Wednesday;
her second beating was after the close of Easter, on a Monday; she was tortured again on the nineteenth of the month of Vardoba;
and her death was on the seventeenth of the month of October, the feast of the holy and blessed martyrs Cosmas and Damian.
And it was a Thursday, the day on which we established the commemoration of Saint Shushanik, to the glory and praise of God,
…of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, to whom glory is fitting forever and ever. Amen.
